1.note: צֶמֶד is a pair or yoke. Read here as "the choicest of their company", rhyming with חֶמֶד; the exact sense is uncertain.

2.note: The question echoes m. Avot 2:9, where Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai asks his five disciples which is the good way a man should cleave to; there too one answer is "a good heart". "Quality" renders מִדָּה, a trait of character.

3.note: Later in this gate עַזּוּת is impudence (zeal without generosity turns to עַזּוּת). Here it may mean boldness or strength; the speaker sets zeal above both humility and its opposite.

4.note: Literally "and it lifts its feet upon their head". Read as wisdom setting the lowly above others; it can also mean that wisdom treads on the heads of the haughty.

5.note: מוּסָר is discipline, moral training and good manners together (Arabic adab). "Good conduct" renders it in this speech and its poem.

6.note: No old man is brought in before this line: the text goes from the seventh youth's poem straight to "the old man". He is Ḥever in disguise, as the end of the gate shows. A line that introduced him may have dropped out, or the author leaves him unannounced.

7.note: The edition prints חֲפָנָיו, "his handfuls", which gives little sense. Translated as if חֲפָצָיו, "his desires" (one letter different).

8.note: That is, every other quality borrows its worth from generosity, as the old man's speech said.

9.note: A pun on the name חֶבֶר (Ḥever) and מְחַבֵּר, "composer", from the same root ("to join").

10.note: The edition points בָּשְׁמוֹ. Read as בְּשָׂמוֹ, "his perfume" (with "to breathe in"), with a play on בִּשְׁמוֹ, "in his name": the scent of his fame.
